scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The 1715 to 1783, 1815 to 1878 and 1920 to present records are linked as a geographic narrative with distinct periods. Their gaps do not mark extinction or founding. Imported polygons remain unchanged; they omit Tobago and are not certified by this content release. No unverified successor links are added.

Banwari’s opening is approximate and is not the date of every find. The National Trust materials disagree on the burial’s age and discovery year, and use changing sex attributions; none is adopted here. The card does not repeat claims of the Caribbean’s oldest skeleton or site, nor infer the precise food ground with each implement.

The first broad phase is a selected regional window, not a single culture or polity lasting thousands of years. The 1592 transition concerns Spanish colonial Trinidad; First Peoples continue and Tobago has a separate colonial history. British capture in 1797 is distinguished from formal cession in 1802.

The original 2014 Rockley report was downloaded and its text read in full for printed pages 12 to 19 after the web reader failed. TRB-5 is associated with the 1677 battle but the identification as Huis te Kruiningen is tentative. Bricks and timbers support a galley interpretation, not a complete reconstructed kitchen. The report’s earliest-fork superlative and contradictory jug numerals are omitted. TRB-2 contains mixed later material and is not used for these dated examples.

NALIS’s general histories contain errors or sweeping claims outside the selected passages. The card excludes the steelpan-only-twentieth-century-instrument claim, a sole inventor, outdated biographies, racial stereotypes, universal household customs, and the attribution of all local seine fishing to Chinese migrants. The emancipation narrative uses the local 1834/1838 distinction, without adopting the source’s incorrect international date list or simplified Haitian leadership account.

The National Archives 1889 proclamation establishes administrative linkage. Other archive pages date later consolidation to 1898 or 1899; the card does not equate all institutional changes or claim complete amalgamation in a single step. The early Trinidad outlines are not presented as evidence that Tobago shared Spanish or early British Trinidad’s government.

Indian arrival in 1845 is not the invention date of all named foods and utensils. The migration range to 1917 is not asserted to be the end date of every existing indenture. Cooking words retain NALIS’s spellings. No food-safety or remedy instructions are included.

The Christmas account describes a practice rather than all residents’ religion or a fixed annual schedule. NALIS’s description of French Patois as broken French is not used. The 2017 Moriah event is explicitly a reenactment, not direct evidence of a specified historical wedding.

The 2023 exhibition documents a living First Peoples community’s participation. Displaying plantains in a modern exhibition does not show that plantains were pre-contact Caribbean crops. No claim of pure, static or vanished Indigenous culture is made.

The solar-oven example is a dated school project from 2015, not an assertion of today’s curriculum or a food-preparation recommendation. Individual children’s names are unnecessary to explain the activity and are omitted.

For independence and republican status, the Office of the President’s institutional history is used. August 1, 1976 is distinguished from the September 24 Republic Day celebration. The card does not repeat misleading claims that independence in 1962 lacked legal sovereignty.

NALIS and the Caribbean Ties article sometimes failed on direct opening; their relevant full indexed passages were read. Ancestral Roots exceeded the web reader’s size limit; its selected historical panel was read in indexed text. This access limitation is distinct from source endorsement.
The new narrative is author-checked against the cited passages and awaits independent historical review.

identityEvidence.assessment: All three historical outlines depict Trinidad alone. The coarse modern outline likewise omits Tobago. Shared narrative coverage follows explicit regional identities and the later named state, without claiming that the imported geometry fully represents it. Tobago examples are separately labelled; neither cultural association nor modern union establishes earlier common sovereignty.

sharedAssociations.basis: The imported outlines cover Trinidad; the later record names the combined state. This regional narrative explicitly separates the islands before their 1889 administrative union and labels Tobago-specific examples. See identityEvidence.
